items.prompt: Black to move. One pawn move guards e5 for a later ...e5 and also opens the road for the bishop on c8. Which pawn move is it?

claims.statement: At depth 16 d6 is the engine's first choice here.
After d6 a black pawn attacks e5.
The alternative ...c5 scores at least 25 cp worse than d6 (depth 16).

hints: Which pawn stands next to the e-pawn and can guard its future square?
The pawn must step to a square that attacks e5 and leaves the c8 bishop a diagonal.
The d-pawn moves one square.
items.explain: The pawn on d6 attacks e5, so a later pawn on e5 is guarded, and the c8 bishop gets the diagonal toward h3. The alternative ...c5 hits d4 at once but gives up the guard of e5; at depth 16 it scores at least 25 cp worse.

feedback_by_move.c7c5: It attacks d4, but after dxc5 Black has no pawn guarding e5 and must win the c5 pawn back.
feedback_by_move.e7e5: The pawn on e5 would be attacked by the pawn on d4 with nothing yet guarding it.

items.prompt: Black plays 5...e5 at once. White exchanges on e5 and the queens come off. Does Black lose a pawn by force?

claims.statement: After 5...e5 the pawn on e5 is attacked twice by White.
It is defended once, by the pawn on d6.
5...e5 scores at least 100 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: Count attackers and defenders of e5 after the pawn arrives there.
After the pawn trade on e5, the two queens face each other on the d-file.
White trades queens with check; Black recaptures with the king and the knight then takes the e5 pawn.
items.explain: After 5...e5 the pawn on e5 is attacked by the pawn on d4 and the knight on f3 and defended only by the pawn on d6. White trades on e5, the queens meet on the d-file, the king has to recapture, and the knight then takes the e5 pawn. At depth 16 5...e5 scores at least 100 cp worse than the best move.

feedback_by_move.no, material stays level: Black's king cannot castle any more after recapturing on d8, and the knight on f3 takes the pawn on e5: nothing defends it, because the bishop on g7 is blocked by its own knight on f6.

items.prompt: Black to move, king castled. Which pawn move challenges White's centre and is the move masters played most here?

claims.statement: At depth 16 e5 is the engine's first choice.
After e5 the pawn on e5 is guarded by the pawn on d6.

hints: Which central pawn of Black has not moved yet?
It attacks the pawn on d4 from the side and is guarded by the pawn on d6.
The e-pawn advances two squares.
items.explain: The e-pawn steps to e5 and attacks d4; the pawn on d6 guards it. In our master games (2500+) 2,491 of the games that reach this position continue with this move. At depth 16 it is the engine's first choice.

items.prompt: White to move. How many black pieces guard the pawn on e5?

claims.statement: Two black pieces guard the pawn on e5.

hints: Count the pawns and pieces that attack e5 from Black's side.
The pawn on d6 is one; look at the knight that came to d7.
The pawn on d6 and the knight on d7: two.
items.explain: The pawn on d6 and the knight on d7 both attack e5; the bishop on g7 is blocked by the knight on f6. So two black units guard the pawn, equal to the two white attackers.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white bishop on g2 attacks (a square holding its own piece counts).

claims.statement: The bishop on g2 attacks exactly these squares.

hints: A bishop moves along diagonals and stops at the first piece it meets.
One diagonal goes down toward f1, the other toward h3, and a third direction runs along the long diagonal.
f1, h1, h3 and f3.
items.explain: The bishop attacks f1 and h1 behind it, h3 in front of the kingside pawns, and f3, where its own knight stands and blocks the long diagonal. The bishop will see the queenside only when that knight moves.

items.prompt: White to move in the Sämisch set-up. Which move keeps the tension and the plan of an attack on the king (two moves are accepted)?

claims.statement: Here 7.d5 and 7.Nge2 are within 40 cp of the first choice (depth 16).
7.dxe5 scores at least 50 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: Which pawn move would release the tension in the centre?
The wanted move keeps the pawn chain or adds a piece to the kingside plan.
The d-pawn advances to d5, or the knight from g1 goes to e2.
items.explain: Both d5 and Nge2 keep the centre closed or tense, so the bishop on e3 and the pawn on f3 stay useful for the attack. Releasing the tension with dxe5 trades queens and scores at least 50 cp worse at depth 16.

feedback_by_move.d4e5: It offers the queen trade, and with the queens off the attack Be3 and f3 were built for is gone.

items.prompt: White plays dxe5, Black retakes with the d-pawn, and White trades queens. Does White come out a pawn ahead?

claims.statement: After the line the engine rates the position at least +1.00 for White (depth 16).
The black king ends on d8.

hints: Where does Black's king stand after the queen trade?
The pawn on e5 is attacked twice and defended once. What can Black try after the knight takes it?
Yes: with the king on d8, Black's trick ...Nxe4 runs into Bg5+.
items.explain: Black has not castled, so the king must recapture on d8 and the pawn on e5 falls. The shot ...Nxe4 does not rescue it, because with the king on d8 the bishop check Bg5+ comes with tempo. The engine (depth 16) puts White at least a full pawn ahead.

items.prompt: White plays dxe5, Black retakes with the d-pawn, and White trades queens. Does White come out a pawn ahead?

claims.statement: After the line the engine rates the position within 0.6 pawn of level (depth 16).
Black's king is on the kingside.
After Nxe5 Nxe4 the engine (depth 16) reads White no better than level: Black regains the pawn.

hints: Where does Black's king stand after the queen trade?
The rook recaptures on d8 and the king keeps its shelter.
No: after the knight takes e5, Black's ...Nxe4 regains the pawn.
items.explain: Black has castled, so the rook, not the king, recaptures on d8. If the knight then takes the pawn on e5, ...Nxe4! and ...Bxe5 regain it, and the engine (depth 16) rates the position within 0.6 pawn of level. The only difference from the last position is the king's square.

items.prompt: White plays dxe5, Black retakes with the d-pawn, and White trades queens. Does White come out a pawn ahead?

claims.statement: After the line the engine rates the position at least +1.00 for White (depth 16).
The black king ends on d8.

hints: Each side has made one a-pawn move before the exchange. Does the king still stand on d8?
The pawn moves on the a-file have nothing to do with the d-file queen trade.
Yes: the same trick works.
items.explain: The extra a-pawn moves, one by each side, change nothing about the king. It is still forced to recapture on d8, and the pawn on e5 still falls; the engine (depth 16) rates it at least +1.00 for White.

items.prompt: Black to move. The knight on f6 attacks the pawn on e4. Does 6...Nxe4 win a pawn?

answer.outcome: no, it loses a piece for a pawn
options: no, it loses a piece for a pawn

claims.statement: One white piece (the knight on c3) defends e4.
6...Nxe4 scores at least 300 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: Count the pieces that attack e4 and the pieces that defend it.
After the knight takes, which white piece can take it back?
The knight on c3 recaptures, and Black has given a knight for a pawn.
items.explain: The knight on f6 attacks e4 once and the knight on c3 defends it once. After 6...Nxe4 White recaptures on e4 and Black has given a knight for a pawn. At depth 16 the capture scores at least 300 cp worse than the best move.

feedback_by_move.yes, a clean pawn: The pawn on e4 is defended by the knight on c3, which recaptures the knight that took it.

A white pawn stands on g3.

hints: Look at the kingside pawns and the long diagonal.
There is a pawn on g3 and a bishop behind it.
The bishop on g2 and the pawn on g3: the Fianchetto, even with the pawn already on e4.
items.explain: A pawn on g3 with the bishop on g2 behind it is the Fianchetto set-up. The signs are g3 and Bg2; the e-pawn may come to e4 later, as it has here.

claims.statement: A white pawn stands on f3.
A white bishop stands on e3.

hints: Look at the f-pawn and the dark-squared bishop.

Pawn f3 and bishop e3: the Sämisch.
items.explain: The pawn on f3 supports e4, the bishop has gone to e3 and the knight to e2, ready for the queen on d2: the Sämisch set-up.

claims.statement: A white bishop stands on e2.
A white knight stands on f3.
A white pawn stands on h3.

hints: Count the white pawns on the fourth rank and look at f2 and g2.
The f-pawn and g-pawn are still at home; the knight is on f3 and the bishop on e2.
Knight f3, bishop e2, kingside pawns at home: the Classical (h3 is a quiet extra).
items.explain: The knight on f3 and the bishop on e2, with the f- and g-pawns at home, are the Classical set-up; h3 is just a useful waiting move.
